title: Topological Sort
tagline: Ordering tasks with dependencies — the algorithm behind build systems, course prerequisites, and package managers.

sections.content:
A **topological sort** of a directed graph is a linear ordering of its vertices such that for every directed edge `u → v`, vertex u comes before vertex v in the ordering. This is only possible on **Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)** — graphs with directed edges and no cycles. If a cycle exists, no valid ordering can be produced.

Topological sort appears everywhere dependency ordering matters: build systems (compile A before B if B depends on A), package managers (install dependencies before the package), course scheduling (take prerequisite before advanced course), and spreadsheet evaluation order. Two classic algorithms solve it — **Kahn's algorithm** (BFS-based, uses in-degree counts) and the **DFS-based approach** (post-order DFS, push to stack on finish). Both run in O(V + E).

sections.title: Building a House
sections.content:
Building a house requires tasks in a strict order: you must pour the foundation before framing, frame before roofing, rough plumbing before drywall. These dependencies form a DAG — no task depends on itself or on a future task (no cycles).

Kahn's algorithm is like a construction manager who checks off tasks as their prerequisites are completed. You start a whiteboard list with all tasks that have *zero* prerequisites (foundation, permits). As each task is completed, you cross off that dependency from successor tasks — any task whose prerequisite count drops to zero is now startable and added to the whiteboard. If every task gets completed this way, you have a valid schedule. If tasks remain on the board with unmet prerequisites, there is a circular dependency — an impossibility.

The DFS approach is like a night-shift worker who explores the dependency chain as deep as possible, then marks tasks as 'scheduled' when returning from their deepest point — last-explored, first-completed.

**Kahn's Algorithm (BFS-based)** works by tracking the **in-degree** of each vertex — the number of incoming edges. Initially, vertices with in-degree 0 have no prerequisites and can be processed first. They are added to a queue. Processing a vertex means removing it from the queue, appending it to the topological order, and decrementing the in-degree of all its neighbors. Any neighbor whose in-degree drops to 0 is added to the queue. If the resulting order contains all V vertices, it is valid. If fewer than V vertices are included, the graph contains a **cycle** — those vertices never reached in-degree 0.

**DFS-based topological sort** runs DFS on all unvisited vertices. When DFS finishes exploring a vertex (all its successors have been fully explored — the *post-order* moment), the vertex is pushed onto a stack. After all DFS calls complete, popping the stack gives the topological order. The correctness intuition: a vertex is pushed only after all vertices reachable from it are already on the stack — so it comes *before* all its successors when the stack is reversed.

**Cycle detection** is a natural byproduct of both approaches. Kahn's detects a cycle if the output has fewer than V vertices (some vertices never had in-degree 0). DFS detects a cycle when it finds a *back edge* — an edge to a vertex already in the current recursion stack (grey, not yet finished). Both run in O(V + E).

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: In-degrees: A=0, B=0, C=2(from A,B), D=1(from B), E=1(from C), F=2(from D,E). Queue starts with [A,B]. Processing A: decrement C (in-degree 1), queue=[B]. Processing B: decrement C to 0 (queue C), decrement D to 0 (queue D). Processing C: decrement E to 0 (queue E). Processing D: decrement F (in-degree 1). Processing E: decrement F to 0 (queue F). Processing F: done. All 6 nodes processed — no cycle.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    INIT["Compute in-degrees for all vertices"]
    INIT --> QUEUE["Enqueue all vertices with in-degree = 0"]
    QUEUE --> PROCESS["Dequeue vertex u, add to order"]
    PROCESS --> DECR["Decrement in-degree of each neighbor v"]
    DECR --> CHECK{"in-degree[v] == 0?"}
    CHECK -->|"Yes"| ENQUEUE["Enqueue v"]
    CHECK -->|"No"| PROCESS
    ENQUEUE --> PROCESS
    PROCESS --> DONE{"Queue empty?"}
    DONE -->|"order.length < V"| CYCLE["Cycle detected"]
    DONE -->|"order.length == V"| VALID["Valid topological order"]
sections.caption: Kahn's algorithm flow: in-degree tracking drives BFS-style processing; cycle detection is a byproduct of the vertex count check.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Kahn's algorithm is usually preferred in practice** because it naturally detects cycles (output size < V) and is easier to reason about iteratively. The DFS approach requires tracking three states (unvisited / in-progress / done) to detect back edges, which is less intuitive. However, DFS topological sort is elegant and memorisable: 'run DFS on every unvisited node, push to stack on exit, reverse the stack'. Both are O(V + E) — choose whichever you can code correctly under pressure.

items: Topological sort produces a linear ordering of a **DAG** where every edge `u → v` has u before v — only possible on graphs with **no cycles**.
**Kahn's algorithm** (BFS-based): compute in-degrees, enqueue zero-in-degree nodes, process and decrement neighbors, detect cycles when output size < V. O(V + E).
**DFS-based sort**: run DFS and push each fully-explored vertex onto a stack (post-order); reverse the stack for topological order; detect cycles via back edges (grey-to-grey edge). O(V + E).
**Cycle detection** is a natural byproduct: Kahn's detects cycles when the output is incomplete; DFS detects them when it finds an edge to a vertex currently on the recursion stack.
Applications include build systems, package managers, course scheduling, spreadsheet formula evaluation — any domain where ordering with dependencies matters.

quiz.question: On what type of graph is topological sort defined?
options: Any connected undirected graph
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) only
Weighted directed graphs with non-negative weights
Complete graphs with V vertices and V*(V-1)/2 edges
quiz.explanation: Topological sort is only possible on Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). If the graph has a cycle, no linear ordering can satisfy the constraint that every edge u→v has u before v — the cycle creates a contradiction (u before v before ... before u).

quiz.question: In Kahn's algorithm, which vertices are added to the initial queue?
options: Vertices with the highest out-degree
Vertices with in-degree equal to 0 (no incoming edges)
Vertices that are neighbors of the source vertex
Vertices in sorted alphabetical order
quiz.explanation: In-degree 0 means no prerequisites — the vertex has no incoming edges and can be processed immediately. These are the 'start' vertices of the DAG. In a course scheduling example, these are courses with no prerequisites. The queue begins with exactly these vertices.

quiz.question: How does Kahn's algorithm detect a cycle in the input graph?
options: By checking for edges that go from right-to-left in the output order
If the output order contains fewer vertices than the total vertex count V
By running DFS after Kahn's completes to verify no back edges
By checking if any vertex has in-degree greater than V/2
quiz.explanation: If the graph has a cycle, the vertices in the cycle never reach in-degree 0 (they always have at least one incoming edge from another vertex in the cycle). They are never enqueued and never appear in the output. So if |output| < V, a cycle exists.

quiz.question: In the DFS-based topological sort, when is a vertex pushed onto the result stack?
options: When DFS first visits the vertex (pre-order)
When DFS finishes exploring all of the vertex's successors (post-order)
When the vertex's in-degree reaches zero
When DFS backtracks to the vertex's parent
quiz.explanation: In DFS topological sort, a vertex is pushed in post-order — after all vertices reachable from it have been fully explored. This ensures that when the stack is reversed, every vertex appears before its successors. Pre-order pushing would give incorrect ordering.

quiz.question: What is a 'back edge' in DFS, and what does finding one mean for topological sort?
options: An edge to an already-visited vertex in a previous DFS call — means the graph has multiple components
An edge to a vertex currently on the recursion stack (marked grey/in-progress) — means the graph has a cycle
An edge going in the reverse direction of the topological order — always safe to ignore
An edge from a vertex with high out-degree to low out-degree
quiz.explanation: A back edge in DFS connects a vertex to an ancestor on the current recursion stack (a 'grey' vertex that is still being explored). This creates a cycle: if u→v is a back edge, there is a path from v to u (via the recursion stack), and now an edge from u back to v — a cycle. Therefore no topological sort is possible.

quiz.question: Graph edges: A→C, B→C, B→D, C→E, D→F, E→F. What is the in-degree of vertex C?
quiz.explanation: In-degree counts incoming edges. C has two incoming edges: A→C and B→C. So in-degree[C] = 2. In Kahn's algorithm, C will not be enqueued until both A and B have been processed and each decrements C's in-degree to 0.

quiz.question: Can a valid graph have more than one correct topological ordering?
options: No — the topological sort of a DAG is always unique
Yes — when independent vertices have no ordering constraint between them, either can come first
Yes — but only when the graph has no edges
Only if all edge weights are equal
quiz.explanation: Multiple valid topological orderings exist whenever two vertices have no dependency relationship between them (neither can reach the other). For example, if A→C and B→C but there is no edge between A and B, both [A,B,C] and [B,A,C] are valid. The queue in Kahn's can dequeue A or B first when both have in-degree 0.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of both topological sort algorithms?
options: O(V log V)
O(V + E)
O(V · E)
O(E log E)
quiz.explanation: Both Kahn's and DFS-based topological sort run in O(V + E). Each vertex is processed once (O(V)) and each edge is examined once (O(E)). This matches standard BFS and DFS complexity — topological sort is essentially a structured traversal.

quiz.question: A build system needs to compile files where file X depends on files Y and Z. If you model this as a graph, what direction should the edge point?
options: X → Y and X → Z (X points to its dependencies)
Y → X and Z → X (dependencies point to X, since they must be compiled first)
The direction doesn't matter — topological sort works either way
Create bidirectional edges between X and its dependencies
quiz.explanation: If Y and Z must be compiled before X, the edges Y→X and Z→X represent 'Y must come before X'. In topological order, Y and Z will appear before X. Alternatively you can use X→Y (X depends on Y) and reverse the topological order. The convention must be consistent — the key insight is that edge direction encodes the 'before' relationship.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes Kahn's algorithm from DFS-based topological sort?
options: Kahn's handles cyclic graphs; DFS only handles DAGs
Kahn's uses a queue and in-degree tracking (BFS-style); DFS-based uses recursion and a post-order stack
DFS-based is O(V+E) but Kahn's is O(E log E)
Kahn's produces exactly one ordering; DFS produces all possible orderings
quiz.explanation: Kahn's is BFS-style: it processes zero-in-degree nodes iteratively, using a queue and counting structure. DFS-based uses recursive depth-first exploration and pushes nodes to a stack in post-order. Both detect cycles (Kahn's by count, DFS by back edges), both are O(V+E), and both can produce multiple valid orderings depending on tie-breaking.
